The promotion of human rights is fundamental to our policy. The Prime Minister was forthright in his statements on human rights during his Asian tour. I have spoken out repeatedly on human rights both here and abroad. We have also taken concrete actions to back up our words.
The Address-Mr. Clark
Last month, we changed our export controls policy to ban the export of military equipment to countries whose governments have a persistent record of violating the human rights of their citizens. On June 12, I reported to the House on the Government's reaction to the report of the Eminent Persons Group of the Commonwealth. In August, the Prime Minister and six other Commonwealth leaders met in London to examine that report and to recommend future actions. All agreed that the authorities in Pretoria had shown no inclination to end apartheid. Six of the countries, including Canada, agreed to put in place a series of 11 measures aimed at inducing the South African Government to reconsider its position.
The United Kingdom agreed separately to implement two national measures and another measure with its European Community partners.
The six of us recommended certain actions and commended our list of measures to the rest of the Commonwealth and to the wider international community, particularly those countries with significant economic relations with South Africa. We have been in touch with those countries directly, the Prime Minister and I, and others. We are pleased that the United States, the European Community and Japan have all announced measures to increase pressure on Pretoria.
At home we are implementing the London program. Some measures, such as the cancellation of the double taxation agreements and the removal of Government assistance to trade and investment, were already in place. In co-operation with the business community we have invoked a ban on new investment and the cessation of bank loans. I have issued notices to importers under the Export and Import Permits Act to prohibit the importing of agricultural products, uranium, coal, iron and steel from South Africa. Implementation of the remaining measures is virtually complete and will be fully effective in the coming weeks. As the House will know I asked that the South Africa Tourist Office close its doors in Canada, and that is being done.
Regarding wheat, Canada is not selling wheat now to South Africa. We have instructed the Wheat Board that there should be no sales to South Africa to take advantage of actions taken by other countries.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to be brief in replying to those questions. The first question deals with the situation of exposure in which countries in front line states find themselves and how we might be able to help. One of the very effective organizations that has been developed in southern Africa is the organization known as SADCC which is comprised of members of the front line states. This year, we are already contributing something in the neighbourhood of $100 million to SADCC and we intend to increase those contributions.
There were discussions at the Commonwealth heads of Government meeting in London as to the steps that might be taken in the event that the reaction of the South African Government was of a kind that caused particular hardship and
disruption in the front line states. While no firm agreement was reached at that time because it was thought that there was a need to have a better idea of what precisely those problems would be, the Prime Minister of Canada volunteered that Canada would be prepared to be active in providing direct financial support to those front line states, although he said that he would prefer it if we were able to act in concert with other countries of the Commonwealth, thinking naturally of Australia and others. We are having active discussions now as to how that can most effectively proceed. That action, were it to be taken, would be in addition to the aid that is now directed toward SADCC.
I should just make one thing more precise. There have been questions raised as to whether or not Canada would be prepared to offer some kind of military support. We would not. In London in early August I had the opportunity to speak at some length with representatives of the African National Congress. I told them that I thought it was essential that they continue to seek peaceful means to bring an end to apartheid, and I indicated that that is very profoundly Canada's desire and would guide actions that we might take with regard to the situation in southern Africa.
With regard to the moratorium, I really should not get ahead of myself in responding to the report of the Joint Committee. I will make an exception in this particular case with respect to the proposal on the moratorium. 1 do not have the exact language of the recommendation in front of me.
Our view, as we begin the week in which Mr. Gorbachev and Mr. Reagan will meet in Iceland, is that the real test in these agreements is to find something to which both sides can comfortably agree. That is not likely to happen in the case of a moratorium so we believe the encouragement that Canada must give is to the United States to continue along the path that was signalled by the President in a speech made to the United Nations two weeks ago today indicating a willingness to now ratify treaties that some months ago the United States was not prepared to ratify. We think that that step-by-step movement toward an end to testing is more likely to be practically effective and, frankly, our interest now, as it has always been, is in seeking measures that will have practical effect.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is an important and legitimate question and one asked frequently across the country. Let me express both a personal view and a government policy, that sanctions rarely work. We are resorting to sanctions in the case of South Africa because we think there is no other instrument that will be effective in causing the regime in South Africa to move away from apartheid.
I have some experience with sanctions, as Hon. Members of the House of Commons may remember, from 1979. Our experience in 1979 was that those sanctions did not in fact have the effect upon the Soviet Union that the Government and, indeed, other Governments implementing them thought would be the case. I will not elaborate by giving more instances of this, but that is generally the case with sanctions. We think that they are generally an ineffective instrument. We believe that in the case of South Africa, nothing else will work and something must work.
If one would ask what distinguishes South Africa from other regimes that conduct practices intolerable and unacceptable to Canadians, I would say there are two things that distinguish South Africa. One, it purports to be a democratic country, as we do, in the way most other countries practising those kinds of violations of human rights do not. Second, it is the only regime in the world that has racial discrimination written into its constitution. Apartheid has that constitutional sanction, and we believe that when South Africa is prepared to incorporate in its law such an offensive principle and is so unprepared to respond to reason in changing it, then we have to resort to actions such as sanctions.
One last word on this. I believe that it might have been possible for people to say that other ways had not been tried adequately before the activities and the report of the Eminent Persons Group. I think any fair observer of events in the world would know that the Eminent Persons, including Archbishop Ted Scott of Canada and others who were drawn together in that work over a long period of time, went to see literally everyone who was interested and effective in that process, came up with reasonable proposals and were not only rebuffed but were rebuffed under circumstances of violence. I think that if a group like that is going to fail, then we must resort to other measures. In this case, the only measures that we think will work are sanctions, and we believe that they have to be applied step by step, gradually increasing the pressure. As I said in my remarks, we are pleased to see that there has recently been movement in the United States, movement in the European community and, importantly, movement in Japan to maintain that pressure which we think and hope will finally lead South Africa to put apartheid behind.

The tradition of the Speech from the Throne is that it provides the Government with an opportunity to set out a new sense of vision, a new sense of direction and a new sense of hope for Canadians. As we in this House are summoned to the other place to have the Speech from the Throne read to us, we look for signs that the Government has been responding to the hopes and aspirations of Canadians as expressed to them over the past couple of years.
I listened with care to the remarks of the Governor General as she read the Speech from the Throne. Unfortunately, that concern and those hopes have not been listened to by this Government. Canadians were looking for a change in direction. Canadians were looking for a new sense of fairness and integrity. Most important, they wanted a sense that the Government recognized their priorities for job creation in

October 6, 1986

tackling the very serious economic crisis facing the country. That was not to be. Canadians were looking for a new direction and for a change. One need look no further than the results of the recent by-elections, the by-election in your own province, Mr. Speaker, the Province of Alberta, in the constituency of Pembina.

-and the results of the by-election in Quebec where the constituents of Saint-Maurice sent a very clear message to the Conservative Government. They said: We, Quebecers, want some change; we want the jobs promised by the Prime Minister two years ago.
Mr. Speaker, I personally canvassed door to door with our candidate Claude Rompre in Quebec. I heard the views of the Quebecers and it was very obvious that they are not at all happy with the policies of the Progressive Conservative Government and that they want some change.
If the people in Saint-Maurice and throughout Quebec heard the throne speech, they were certainly very disappointed because it does not promise any change. It promises the same direction and reflects the same lack of respect for priorities and for people not only in Quebec, but throughout Canada.

I want to say a word about the process of the Speech from the Throne as we all traipse down to the other place, stand there and listen in awe in the plush surroundings of the Senate Chamber with its collection of hacks, flacks, bagmen and cronies of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), which surely constitutes an embarrassment in a democratic society. Some of us ask ourselves if it is not about time to abolish the institution, abolish the Senate and put an end to the charade of these appointees of Prime Ministers making decisions that vitally affect the lives of ordinary Canadian men and women.

October 6, 1986

In the Province of British Columbia today we have a Premier who says the same thing. He says that everything is fantastic and that this is a piece of cake. The people of British Columbia know better. They know that what we want in the Province of British Columbia is action-action on unemployment, action on cut-backs in health care, and action on cutbacks in education.
Let us look at education for a minute. We have a federal Government which is cutting back on transfer payments to the province and cutting back on education. Also we in British Columbia have a Minister who has the audacity to suggest that poor people should think twice before going on to pursue post-secondary education. Yesterday the Social Credit Minister responsible for post-secondary education suggested that poor people should examine their priorities and consider putting off post-secondary education if they are unable to afford it. What kind of approach is that from Bill Vander Zalm, Rus Fraser, and their Social Credit colleagues to accessibility to post-secondary education in the Province of British Columbia? What he is saying to the poor is to forget it, that if they cannot afford a decent education, they should not bother applying to college or university. We in the New Democratic Party who have fought for years and decades for universal access to quality education will not accept that approach. We believe that there must be a change, and I am confident that there will be a change in the Province of British Columbia after October 22.
We are looking as well-and I am speaking now from the perspective of a Member of Parliament from British Columbia-at the whole question of fairness and equity for women. We are looking at the whole question of pay equity and legislation, enforceable legislation which will ensure that women are not treated as second-class citizens in the workforce. Recently we saw legislation on employment equity tabled in the House which left a great deal to be desired. It was toothless legislation with no enforcement mechanisms whatsoever.
As well, we see in the Province of British Columbia a Social Credit Government working hand in glove with the Mulroney Conservatives-

One of the most important industries in the country-and it is by far the most important industry in the Province of British Columbia-is the forestry industry. We have seen a succession of promises made and broken by the federal Government. We are awaiting effective action in the forestry sector. We know that our forests are being destroyed and that there is not adequate reforestation. We call upon the Government to put

money into effective reforestation programs. Instead, we have more studies and no action. I am proud of the fact that in the Province of British Columbia Bob Skelly, the Leader of the provincial New Democratic Party, has said that we would work with a federal Government which takes its responsibilities seriously in this important area, and that we would create thousands upon thousands of jobs in the forestry sector through effective reforestation schemes. That is the kind of approach to job creation which we as New Democrats support and in which we believe.
There are those people who ask where we will get the money from for these job creation programs. I will tell the House where we will get the money from. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) clearly documented the fact that thousands and thousands of corporations in Canada are not paying one penny in income tax despite the fact that they are making very great profits on a year to year basis. It is about time that we got serious about tax reform and recognized that the corporate sector should be paying its fair share of taxes. That is one source of funds which the Government could use to create jobs. Another source is the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption. Whom does this benefit? It directly benefits those who are the wealthiest, those who are the most affluent in society. Of course that creates no jobs at all for the people of British Columbia or for the people of Canada.
Another area in which there should be changes is the whole area of waste in government advertising. For example, we have seen in the Province of British Columbia some $20 million being spent by Bill Vander Zalm and the Socreds on blatant political advertising at the expense of British Columbia taxpayers. Instead of taking taxpayers' money and spending it in that kind of arbitrary way to promote re-election, we suggest that the money should be taken and put into effective job-creation programs.
One example of that is the youth job guarantee program which has been suggested by my provincial colleagues in British Columbia and by Bob Skelly, the Leader of my Party. As well, it has been actively supported by the outstanding team of NDP candidates in British Columbia, people like Joan Sawicki in Burnaby-Willingdon, Ron Johnson in Burnaby- Edmonds, and Barry Jones in Burnaby North. They are talking about working on priorities to create jobs and about a youth job guarantee program. The suggestion is that we are failing our young people in the country by not allowing them to have any hope, by not providing any optimism, and by not providing any sense of vision for the future. The youth job guarantee program says that when one reaches 17 years or 18 years of age, one will have the option of being able to pursue post-secondary education, of having a job, or of being able to go into some sort of training to help find a job. It is that kind of guarantee which will help to create hope and a sense of confidence in our young people in British Columbia and throughout the land. It is that kind of inspired leadership by my provincial colleagues which I am hoping will lead to real job creation in the Province of British Columbia.

October 6, 1986
The Address-Mr. Robinson
In my capacity as justice critic for the federal New Democratic Party, I want to touch for a moment-and I know that time is limited-on a number of issues on which we will be looking for action in the upcoming session of Parliament. We hope the Government will take effective action to deal with the very serious concerns of Canadians, particularly those in the Maritimes who recognize the inequities in Canada's current laws on abortion. In both the Province of Prince Edward Island and the Province of Newfoundland there are no facilities whatsoever for women who seek access to safe therapeutic abortions. Surely that kind of situation represents a denial of equality to women and must be changed.
We are also looking for effective action on changes to the Canadian Human Rights Act. The Government has promised that changes will be made. We hope that these changes to strengthen the protections accorded minorities in Canada and to look at the whole area of systemic discrimination will be made in the very near future.
We must look at the crisis facing the Canadian prison system. We in Canada imprison far too many people for far too long. Our prisons are over-crowded. We see double bunking in many cases and we see the spectacle of prisons being built in the country as job-creation projects far from the families of prisoners and far from qualified professional staff. Once again that is unacceptable.
The Prime Minister has spoken of his war on drugs and the drug epidemic in Canada. All Canadians share in the concern over the abuse of drugs in our society. However, I suggest that we have to look very seriously at the abuse not only of illegal drugs but of perhaps the most destructive drug of all, that being alcohol. How many of our families have not been touched by alcoholism? We know, for example, that alcohol has caused tremendous waste and human suffering. Some 66 per cent of fatal accidents in Canada are alcohol-related. Over half the suicides among young people involve alcohol. A great proportion of accidents in the home are alcohol-related. I could go on and on about the destructiveness of alcohol, so when the Prime Minister talks about a war on drugs, let us ensure that he is prepared to take action with respect to the abuse of alcohol as well.
Let us also hope that he looks very seriously at the archaic laws dealing with marijuana. Under these laws today our young people can still go to jail or receive a criminal record for possession. Changes to those laws are long overdue.
There are a number of other concerns. We have the matter of sexual abuse of young people. Our freedom of information and privacy legislation remains far too weak. The Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General is studying this legislation and we hope the Government will move to strengthen it significantly.
Dealing with pornography, we hope the Government does not come back with the kind of repressive, sledge-hammer
legislation which totally fails to distinguish between erotica and violent, degrading pornography. I think the Government may have gotten the message, but it is important that it not yield to the forces of reaction, the dinosaurs in the Tory back benches, who insist that the previous Bill be brought back intact. We will await with interest the government response in this area.
You are signalling, Mr. Speaker, that my time is just about up with respect to this response to the Speech from the Throne. I just want once again to indicate how important we in British Columbia view the next two years to be. The Government was given an overwhelming mandate, not just by the people of Canada but also by the people of British Columbia, and so far the Government has blown it. It has not responded to the concerns of the people of British Columbia about job creation, or fairness and integrity in Government. We in the NDP intend to continue fighting on behalf of the concerns of ordinary Canadians, ordinary British Columbians, together with our colleagues at the provincial level, people such as Bob Skelly of the provincial NDP. We hope that together there will be real changes, both federally and provincially.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to take part in this debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. Before proceeding I should like to extend my most sincere congratulations to the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) on his election as Speaker of the House of Commons. I wish him well in the discharge of this onerous responsibility and I want to express my full respect and confidence.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I would now like to tell my distinguished House colleagues and all Canadians, especially the people of my riding of Jonquiere whom I humbly represent, about the various points which drew my attention during the Speech from the Throne delivered by Her Excellency the Governor General, the Right Hon. Jeanne Sauve. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, the people of Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean were honoured to play hosts to Her Excellency the Governor General on the occasion of her short stay in our region last week. She is an extraordinary lady to whom I pay my respect. During her visit in our region she expressed particular concern about the way ordinary people look upon politicians. She stated that in many cases people do not think kindly of men and women in politics, yet the only aspiration of these men and women is their will and desire to serve.
The remark is very relevant and the Governor General is indeed an eloquent representative to convey such a message to Canadian men and women with respect to the world of politics.
In response to the various issues raised in the Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, allow me to quote an article published in last Thursday's La Presse and signed by editorial writer Michel Roy:
A fresh start
he wrote.
The Speech from the Throne opening the second session of the Mulroney Government highlights both continuity and change.
Continuity, because again it features the major themes advocated by the same Government in its 1984 legislative program, namely national reconciliation and economic renewal;
Change, because Mr. Mulroney and his colleagues focus on a perspective they had neglected two years earlier: the social policies which mean so much to Canadians.
Considering the balance he was able to give to his speech, balance between economic and social priorities as well as national and international issues, the Prime Minister proves that he has a clearer view of the expectations of Canadians. The shift towards social matters and the large number of concrete measures announced in the speech, from tax reform to day care centres, reflect a new realism.
The legislative program is full of possibilities.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, what are these new policies the Government intends to advocate during the second session? A radical change has to be our firm intention to give special consideration to new social measures.
The new policy on daycare centres, to be implemented following the tabling of a report by the committee responsible for studying needs in this area, is one example of our resolve to be progressive in terms of family policy.
Improvements in pension plans, an adjustment program for older workers, measures to promote volunteer work, the Government's firm resolve to take effective measures against child sexual abuse, violent forms of pornography involving women and children, child prostitution, and the grave and growing threat posed by the trafficking in illegal drugs, will all be on the legislative agenda in the months to come. These, and many other social policies such as those relating to the intolerable affront to human dignity suffered by battered women, compel the Government's commitment to work with the provinces to implement the most effective means and methods of action in response to the concerns of the Canadian people.
Other important issues were raised in the Speech from the Throne, announcing the Government's firm intentions of developing new policies and injecting additional funds for promoting research and setting up a national advisory board for industrial technology and improving the quality of postsecondary education, with a view to achieving excellence and providing equal opportunity. Similarly, active internationalism and increasing trade remain an absolute priority.
The Opposition may be fond of showering criticism on the free trade talks, but if we fail to conclude bilateral agreements on the various activity sectors in our respective economies, Canada's economy is in grave danger of being partially paralyzed. And all because of the increasing number of protectionist measures now being put before the U.S. Congress. The trend is growing and may result in the loss of many jobs. Mr. Speaker, the answer is clear: negotiate. Justice and good faith still have their place, and I believe that between friendly countries, agreement is always possible.
Canada's exports to the United States are worth more than $94 billion, while U.S. exports to our country are worth about $75 billion annually. The stakes are high, since millions of jobs depend on the outcome, and every time the Americans impose new protectionist measures, men and women stand to lose their jobs. The Opposition has taken a very negative stand, but I remain convinced that the talks offer a better perspective than doing nothing or just letting things happen.
Further, Mr. Speaker, an agreement inviting Quebec to take the honourable route towards becoming an active partner in the Canadian Constitution remains one of our major objectives and we hope this agreement will be ratified as soon as possible.
And what about the trend towards adjusting our policies and programs in terms of specific regional needs? This desire to
October 6, 1986

take into account the differences and specific needs of all of our regions should not be just a case of Government priorities and policies. It should also be the objective of our major businesses and our Crown corporations, which should adapt their expansion and investment policies to regional differences and disparities.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention one example, the position taken by Bell Canada which this summer, through its director general, announced to the people of Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean that the company intended to allow for the regional entity in its policies for the development of regional services, instead of considering various aspects such as the community of interests and distance or contiguity, and that it would consider local conditions in every region. In fact, a region consists of municipalities, and when we talk about developing regional services as opposed to inter city services, we must try to increase the cohesiveness of the towns within the region. And Bell Canada's President himself did recognize that principle, that is the importance of regional association, and Bell has agreed in the Saguenay area to have a pilot study conducted for the purpose indeed of finally regrouping all communities in the Saguenay MRC. This will be a first, Mr. Speaker, and I am very happy with Bell's new outlook. I also urge the CRTC, when the time comes, to change the parameters so that from now on, when talking about developing regional service, the actuel needs of the population be addressed and the regions be taken into account.
Mr. Speaker, other major changes were announced, including tax reform. A first measure already has become law, imposing a minimum tax. Accordingly, 79,000 more Canadians will be paying taxes, people who until now have succeeded in paying none, availing themselves of all kinds of tax deductions. These loopholes have now been plugged by our Government. And soon the tax reform will simplify our tax returns and lead to lower income tax for many Canadian men and women, a highly desirable goal, Mr. Speaker.
All in all, this is a promising Throne Speech, the key elements of which will be introduced over the coming weeks and months as so many pieces of legislation.
At the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I quoted from a columnist, Mr. Michel Roy, who referred both to changes and to continuity in the Throne Speech of this our thirty-third Parliament. Continuity refers to what has been started. And if I may, I would like to remind Hon. Members of the numerous achievements of this Government and the progress made in terms of economic performance.
Much too often, Mr. Speaker, we are criticized and even taken to task, I would say. The nit-picking is so well schemed that people lose perspective. But our record is impressive. I could mention national reconciliation recalling that the provinces seldom had such good relations with the Canadian Government. What a change from the arrogance and contempt that prevailed for years!
The Address-Mr. Blackburn
Our Government has also reached a number of sectorial agreements with the provinces, for instance sectorial agreements on transportation, and my own region, Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean, will be benefitting, to the tune of $25 million provided by the Quebec Government and the Canadian Government, actually towards a project in our area, the Alma-La Baie expressway. Those $25 million will not be enough, but a major hurdle has been passed with that agreement entered upon by our two Governments.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to speak about the Canadian Jobs Strategy, which emphasizes training and co-operation with the private sector and programs to create permanent jobs with a training element. Among the employment development programs, let me mention Challenge '86, under which students can find a summer job in their own field of study to help them to innovate and acquire new qualifications, and so on. Several billions of dollars have been invested in these job creation programs in the last two years.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, our strategy is bearing fruit since the unemployment rate has gone down from 11.7 per cent to under 10 per cent in two years to reach 9.7 per cent last August. We are creating nearly four times as many jobs in a month as the previous Government. Our Government is creating nearly
25,000	new jobs each month.
As for the interest rates, they have also gone down under 10 per cent, and the inflation rate has decreased and is still at about 4 per cent. These are all good economic results and we shall go on as we have begun.
According to the OECD, Canada will have the highest employment increase this year among major industrialized country and the second best rate among the 25 member countries of the OECD. As for the economic performance in my own region and in my constituency of Jonquiere, it is also positive. For instance, there is the pulp and paper company Abitibi Price, in which $150 million have been invested to modernize facilities and produce a new type of fine paper. This is encouraging and shows confidence in the economic future of our region and our country. Three plants, Cascades, Abitibi Price and Alcan, employ nearly 8,000 people or 19 per cent of the labour force in the Jonquiere constituency, which greatly depends on a vigorous market for aluminum and for pulp and paper.
It is easy to see that economic recovery is essential for the welfare of our regions and that our policies must take regional disparities and differences into account. We need to have a complementary approach to diversify the economy of each region in the country, and the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region is no exception to the rule.
At this point, I would like to point to SOCCRENP, a business sponsorship corporation set up recently, thanks to the co-operation of big business and small-and medium-sized businesses in our region and the two levels of government. The corporation's goal is to stimulate the creation of new businesses in the region. Last week, the first business created with

October 6, 1986
The Address-Ms. Copps
the help of SOCCRENP was launched, under the name Spectube. The business is in fact concerned with aluminum processing.
It is very encouraging to see the business world taking the initiative. I think we can expect a great deal from this kind of corporation, whose objective is also to create businesses and thus create jobs.
Mr. Speaker, there are many other priorities in the riding of Jonquiere, and as the Member for this riding, I am working very hard to deal with them. Some examples are relocating the post office in Jonquiere or relocating the employment centre. It has been several months, Mr. Speaker, that I started working on this file, and I don't intend to drop it, because all this is very important to my riding, since it is a matter of improving services for my constituents.
A second important issue is the rationalization of railway transportation in the Upper Saguenay, which will mean removing certain tracks which are no longer being used in the Jonquiere area. This is another important matter on which I am working very hard. Today, negotiations are going on between Canadian National, VIA Rail and Roberval-Sague-nay to reach an agreement, and I expect to make some major progress very shortly.
In any case, I am prepared to use all my energy and effort in the defence of the interests of the people of the riding of Jonquiere and to promote its economic development.
Mr. Speaker, I have every confidence in this Government which has clearly shown its desire to listen to the regions and do everything it can to distribute economic wealth more equitably in this country.

Mr. Speaker, first and foremost I should like to thank and congratulate all those who have already taken part in this debate, particularly the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I should also like to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, for your commendable effort during the election which lasted until two o'clock in the morning.
We had an extra month, Mr. Speaker, to kind of get back to reality. I think a lot of us in the House of Commons, both on the government side and the opposition side, realize that we sometimes get caught up in the politics of Parliament Hill and forget what the people back in the ridings are saying. In this particular instance, we had the benefit of one extra month because the Government was going to go back to the people, back to the drawing board, back to the grass roots and find out what the people were really saying about the first two years of the greatest mandate in the history of Canada. In fact, this
month would have been well spent had we seen a specific response in the Speech from the Throne to some of the concerns being expressed by Canadians. Forgive me, Mr. Speaker, if I am a little cynical, but it was almost like deja vu. When I was in the Ontario Legislature I used to read the recorded ruminations of people like Norm Atkins. He used to write beautiful speeches for the Premier of Ontario who was very successful at being all things to all people in all parts of Ontario. It was almost "Campkaesque", the fine imprint of the Dalton Camps of this world, that we could see written all over that Speech from the Throne. We have a Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who is responding to women's issues, to drug abuse, to alchoholism, to the economy, to the unemployment problem. He is going to be all things to all people. Frankly, I think we should congratulate him, except for one fatal flaw. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) knows I would bring in the one fatal flaw.

A few weeks later, he gets elected and the first thing he does is to run out and hire a nanny at the taxpayers' expense. But she is not really a nanny. She is a staff person who interfaces with the children on a habitual basis. 1 will be able to speak shortly from first-hand experience, and I would love to have a staff person who interfaces with the children on a habitual basis. Let us call a nanny a nanny. Let us call a butler a butler. Let us call a maid a maid. 1 think my hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), made a moot point when he suggested that he did not realize the Prime Minister's underwear had become an issue of national security. The Prime Minister said he absolutely had to have a valet and a maid on his trip to the Far East for security reasons, even though he had an RCMP officer, among others, who was there simply to watch the bags and to make sure there was in fact no security breach. It now becomes part of public policy that the maid and the valet have to follow the Prime Minister around.
In the last session, when it was revealed that the taxpayers of Canada paid for a Hercules for a film crew to travel around and catch every last precious moment of the fleeting mandate of this Prime Minister, the pay-off for that came from the taxpayers, and the Prime Minister again cited reasons of security. It seems to me again that while he talks about budgets and cut-backs, the Prime Minister intends to continue the practice he began increased his own office staff by some 54 per cent when he was first elected. We hear rumours and press reports that now it is not enough for each of the Ministers to have a chauffeur. There are now certain Ministers in the Government-and its back-benchers will want to hear this- who want their assistants to have chauffeurs. It is not enough that their chief politicos have a salary increase which is far higher than the average Canadian would have received, but certain of their assistants believe they should have chauffeur-driven limousines to carry them about.

I think it is important that the government back-benchers be aware that this is the same Government which is preaching Fiscal restraint. It is the same Government which said in the Speech from the Throne that it wants to introduce new measures of fiscal responsibility. There is an election going on in Saskatchewan. What has the Government done with respect to wheat subsidies? We have heard nothing specific in the Speech from the Throne. There was nothing definitive. It takes a 5.30 a.m. phone call by the Premier of Saskatchewan who on bended knees said: "Please help me out, because if you do not, you will not be able to count on us in the next election". It is the height of cynicism for the Prime Minister to announce the withdrawal of the PGRT only because of a by-election. It is the height of cynicism for the Prime Minister to announce wheat payments which will come from existing funds. He is merely shuffling the deck. That is the height of cynicism.

Mr. Speaker, referring to the files which I have been asked to study as Party critic, we discovered among other things that older workers are hardest hit by the unemployment climate in Canada. We know that, even since the end of the recession, the number of unemployed workers over 50 has doubled, which means that these people do not find work, all they find is despair.
We remember quite well that about a year ago, in the month of February when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tabled his famous Budget, he promised he would replace the LAB program, the Labour Adjustment Benefits program.
They cancelled that program and promised that as early as August 1986 we would have a new program specifically designed for unemployed older workers.
He proposed that he would introduce a new program for older workers by August of 1986. We now see that he is reannouncing the same program for older workers.

This is exactly the same program which was promised in February when they dropped the Liberal program for older workers which had been in existence before.
How can people believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who is telling us in his Speech from the Throne that he will give us the very same policies we have had for two years? Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
October 6, 1986
The Address-Ms. Copps
Speaker, we already know that the polls reveal that Canadians are wary of the Prime Minister's word, they do not believe him anymore because he tricked them too often, saying one thing to some people and something else to others.

The public is sceptical, with good reason. If we look to the area of housing, which is another area within my responsibilities as critic, there is not a single mention in the Speech from the Throne with respect to the plight of the thousands of Canadian homeless who will be facing a very cold winter. What we have seen again is the divestment-

The Government is shirking its responsibilities towards the provinces because the federal Government does not want to provide the housing services such as had been promised by the former Liberal administration.
For example, if we look at British Columbia-

We know that the Government in British Columbia is not committed to social housing. In fact, I was shocked to hear the words of the Minister responsible for education in British Columbia who said that he felt that maybe poor people should rethink sending their families to college or university.
I would like to take a few moments to tell the House why my family and I became Liberals. My father was one of six boys raised by a widow in northern Ontario back in the mid-1920s. At that time my grandmother was struggling as a court stenographer to raise her six children. She was anxious to send one of them to school, but she did not have the money to pay for the examination which had to be taken to follow up on post-secondary education. She wrote to the Minister responsible for education in the Province of Ontario at that time and said: "I am a widow with six sons. I would like to send at least one of them, who wants to be a veterinarian, to school so that he can achieve his goal". The Conservative Minister at the time wrote my grandmother and said: "Madam, in your circumstances I think it is highly outrageous that you should even consider sending any of your sons to a post-secondary institution". My grandmother became an ardent Liberal from that day forward. She believed that any Government, including the Socred Government of British Columbia or the Conservative Government then in Ontario, which would say to poor people that you cannot afford education and that there should not be universal accessibility to it, should not get her vote. I think this political philosophy is a hallmark of what we are seeing here in Ottawa.
With respect to housing, I received a letter today, and I think other Members will be receiving ones in the same vein. They should be aware of the new housing policies of the Government which targets the so-called core needy. The letter I received was from Dora Hilton who lives in Whitby, Ontario. She received a rent increase of 50 per cent in 1985 and another rent increase of 50 per cent in 1986. She is a senior citizen who,
in just two years, has had her rent increased by 100 per cent. Her rent is now almost $500 a month. The people in her building are extremely upset, but this is the dilemma they face. They have no place to go. Through its sad omission of any reference to housing in the Speech from the Throne the Government has shown it is abandoning a national strategy for housing. It is content to leave the question of housing up to the provinces. I am sure we will have a chance to say more about this subject in the future. However, I draw the matter to the attention of Hon. Members because I think there is a national crisis in terms of housing. Anyone who lives in a major urban centre will be aware of the crisis. Frankly, they will be shocked, as am I, that the Government has made no reference to it in the Speech from the Throne.
As the only opposition Member in the area of Hamilton, the lone voice of Opposition now that the former Member for Hamilton Mountain has departed-

There are certain issues currently taking place in the Hamilton area which bear national scrutiny. One deals with the Hamilton airport.
Terminal 1 at the Toronto Airport is in a state of absolute crisis. Most Members have probably been through Terminal 1, and I ask Hon. Members whether or not they agree that Terminal 1 is a disaster area. Terminal 1 is a joke. It is an insult to any person arriving on an international flight who is en route to the southwestern Ontario area. I agree that we need to do something about the overcrowding problem. At the same time, only a few kilometers away in the City of Hamilton there is a beautiful $50 million facility which is lying waste. It was cited by the Auditor General as being one example of our not receiving value for our dollar. It just does not have the necessary passenger loads.
Before the daily trips to Vancouver last summer the total number of passengers travelling through the Hamilton airport was 40. At the same time we were seeing an overload of 4 million passengers only a few kilometers away in the City of Toronto. The then Minister of Transport attended an emergency meeting at the time. He very kindly agreed to receive our Mayor and our Regional Chairman who laid out the problem to him. He was sympathetic, as only he can be. Heaven knows, at times he can be sympathetic and at times he can need our sympathy. We are never quite sure which it is. Nonetheless, he was sympathetic. He said that he would do something about the problem. Only a few days later he issued a press release in which he said that he was proud to announce that he was giving permission to another airline to land at Terminal 1 in the City of Toronto. That airline is TAP of Portugal.
October 6, 1986

It seems to me that if there is one facility which is lying waste and another which is completely crowded to capacity, then this is an unimaginable situation for anyone who has experienced it on Sunday, Monday or Tuesday night. Why did the Minister of Transport not say to TAP that we would be very happy to see it land in southwestern Ontario but that it will have to be at Hamilton and not Toronto? There are many people living in the vicinity of the Hamilton area. We are the hub of the golden horseshoe and not that far from Toronto. It would certainly be easy to set up a shuttle service between the two airports, thus permitting people who want to fly beyond the southwestern Ontario area to proceed to their connections. However, there is a Minister who really revealed his true colours when he went to Atlantic Canada and told Atlantic Canadians that they should stop complaining because they have it better than those in Bangladesh or Sri Lanka. He said the same thing when he came to Hamilton. He said he would deal with our concerns and try to assist the airport, but within the short space of a few days he agreed to let another airline into Toronto while this particular airport is being neglected.
There is one reason for this, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps I could give some positive advice to the Prime Minister. Those in Hamilton need a cabinet Minister from the Hamilton area. The Minister who is currently designated as the Minister for Hamilton is the Hon. Member from Oakville. His designation escapes me because he comes to Hamilton so seldom that no one even knows who he is. I am sure that if I were to ask 10 people at Jackson Square who the Minister responsible for Hamilton is, they would not know that it is the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek). I suppose that is the only association he has with Hamilton. We do have a good football team and shortly we will have an NHL franchise.

someone who speaks forcefully in the House of Commons, how many jobs have been lost in the footwear industry as a result of the devastating Tory policy that was passed in the House of Commons a year ago. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had the pleasure of participating in a footwear task force which travelled through southwestern Ontario. speechtext:
Today I have been given the opportunity to speak on the Throne Speech, a task I undertake with conviction and confidence. The Throne Speech is not a detailed plan of action, it is a statement of intent. Therefore, a true assessment of the impact of a Throne Speech can only be determined by an examination of the Government's record following the speech.
On November 4, 1984, the Governor General presented the first Throne Speech of this Government setting a theme of national reconciliation, economic renewal and social justice. In the 23 months following that speech, much has already been accomplished toward those goals, even as we recognize the long road ahead, if we are to achieve the lofty aims that we have set for ourselves. That is why I am especially pleased to see that last week's Throne Speech did not forget the promises we made, but renewed our commitment to achieving their fulfilment.
One of the important commitments made in both speeches was the achievement of economic equality for women. In order to allow women the opportunity to attain their full economic potential, we must ensure that women have equal access to employment and opportunities to advance to the most senior levels of management. The adoption of the employment equity principle outlined in the Abella Report is a prime example of the Government's commitment to full equality for women. We have acted to ensure that Crown corporations, federally regulated businesses and private companies which have contracted to do business with the Government give women better job opportunities. In just two years the Government has increased the percentage of women appointed to federal boards and commissions to over 25 per cent from the previous Government's record of 15 per cent. Our Government has made good on its commitment to improving economic opportunities for women in Canada. The facts speak for themselves. Since September, 1984 unemployment among women has fallen by 90,000, a record on which this Government is seeking to build.
The future of young Canadians is being addressed as well. We have dedicated ourselves to working with the provinces and the private sector to enhance job opportunities for our young people. We are committed to encourage initiative and the entrepreneurial spirit among the youth. A few months ago I received a letter from a young student who was interested in pursuing a career in scientific research. He requested my advice on the likelihood of career opportunities in his chosen field. Looking to the Throne Speech, I answer him with a resounding yes. There is a future for those seeking a career in the scientific or high-tech fields. We have committed ourselves to expanding opportunities for the future. Once again, the figures confirm our commitment to Canadian youth. The record shows that since September, 1984, unemployment among youth has fallen by 109,000. We are backing up our promises with action.
The Address-Mr. Witer
Parkdale-High Park is an urban riding with a population of approximately 92,000. While the unemployment rate in our constituency runs at about 4.7 per cent, we do not consider ourselves to be free of difficulties. We have worked hard to achieve that rate, and the response to my householder questionnaire indicates that unemployment is one of the single most important concerns of my constituents.
There is no doubt that we have benefited from programs such as the Canadian Jobs Strategy and Challenge 86 which have contributed to our relatively low unemployment rate. Since 1985, the Government has allocated $900 million over and above the resources already available for training and employment programs to implement the Canadian Jobs Strategy. During the past two years, the total number of unemployed has dropped by 215,000, with the unemployment rate dropping a full 2 percentage points from 11.7 per cent in September, 1984, to 9.7 per cent in August, 1986. The Government recognizes that those percentage points translate into real people who face very serious hardship in providing for the needs of their families. Whether the rate of unemployment is 9.7 or 4.7, Canadians deserve and demand the right to provide for their needs with dignity. Percentage points are insignificant to someone who does not have a job.
In the 23 months since our election we have created 563,000 jobs, 80 per cent of which are full time. The OECD forecasts that Canada will have the largest rate of employment growth of any major industrialized nation this year. That is the record of our Government, the record on which this Throne Speech promises to build.
The Government has recognized in this Throne Speech and, indeed, in the previous one, that Canada does not exist in a vacuum. We cannot hope to create the economic opportunities we seek for Canada without looking to our trading partners. That is why we have undertaken negotiations with the United States to open up opportunities for freer trade between our two nations. We are determined to open up trade opportunities not only in the United States but with Japan and other Pacific Rim countries.
Our efforts to attract investment to Canada as a source of jobs has not gone unrewarded. In the automotive sector alone since 1985, Hyundai, Toyota, Honda and General Motors have all announced plans to build plants in Canada. We are committed to building on these success stories by continuing to encourage investment and development in Canada.
Our involvement in the international community brings with it responsibility and opportunity. The Throne Speech underscores our efforts to take an active role in world affairs. In 1988, leaders of the seven major industrialized nations will meet in Canada for the annual economic summit. Our admission to the Group of Seven has given Canada a unique opportunity to take a leading role in world economic affairs.

October 6, 1986
The Address-Mr. Witer

With Quebec and New Brunswick, we set the stage for the very first francophone summit, and now Canada will host the second summit in 1987.

Also in 1987, we will be hosting the Commonwealth Conference in Vancouver. Canada has played a major role in the Commonwealth over the years. Our membership has provided us with an important tool for exerting our influence in world affairs. Our efforts to abolish apartheid in South Africa is an example of the leading role Canada has taken within the Commonwealth.
Canada has an obligation to the international community to expose the gross violations of basic human rights in all countries including the Soviet Union where freedom of movement, freedom of speech, and freedom of religious belief are restricted and denied and where families have been cruelly separated by the refusal of passports for those seeking to join relatives in the West. Canada has been in the forefront of the fight to maintain basic human rights for all.
The measures which the Government has taken against South Africa; the pressure which has been exerted by the Canadian Government on the Soviet Union in order to free dissidents such as Shcharansky, Orlov, Danylo Shumuk, Oksana Meshko, Viktoras Petkus and others; and the representations made during the recent visit of the Soviet Foreign Minister have all had as their aim the restoration of human rights to those who have been denied them. We have spoken out for those who cannot speak for themselves.
Our participation in the United Nations is central to Canadian foreign policy and has allowed us to press our position on such issues as verifiable arms reductions and human rights violations to an even larger international audience. My trip last year to the United Nations General Assembly in New York afforded me the chance to study the institution more closely. I am pleased to note Canada's renewed commitment to the UN. Through the UN, Canada has taken a leading position in pushing for verification of existing arms control agreements and for the negotiation of new accords. Verification is not an obstacle but is an essential component of any solution to disarmament issues. Our renewed commitment to the UN will allow us to continue efforts to strengthen the UN's capacity, to investigate allegations of non-compliance, and to expand UN involvement in the formation and execution of verification provisions.
My constituency of Parkdale-High Park has a vibrant and vocal ethnocultural community. Recent statistics show that some 60 per cent of my constituents have an ethnocultural heritage. Canada's commitment to a multicultural mosaic has provided this country with a rich and unique character and has made an invaluable contribution to Canadian society.
The Government has initiated a number of key accomplishments in the field of multiculturalism. One of the highlights was the first ever federal-provincial-territorial conference on
multiculturalism which was convened in 1985. The conference was an unqualified success, and the Government has since gone on to establish the House of Commons Standing Committee on Multiculturalism.
My constituents have expressed concern over Canada's refugee policy. I am pleased that their concerns have been addressed in the Throne Speech. The reforms as outlined in the Throne Speech will produce a system which is both fair and effective. It will assist genuine refugees in need of protection and discourage abuse of Canada's humanitarian tradition. It was the promise of freedom and justice which brought all of us to Canada. It is the fulfilment of that promise which makes us proud to be Canadians.
In order to fulfil that promise of freedom and justice, the Throne Speech addressed many important issues in the area of social justice. We have undertaken to remove barriers which have prevented women from participating freely and equitably in the mainstream of Canadian society. We have resolved to take effective action against child abuse, pornography, child prostitution, and the growing threat of illegal drug traffic. The Throne Speech has addressed the major concerns of my constituents. It has addressed the concerns of the region and of all Canadians.
Members of Parliament cannot limit their concerns and interests to issues which only affect those residing within the arbitrarily drawn electoral boundaries. Our responsibility lies in representing the people of our province and of our country. It is incumbent upon all of us to discuss issues and to make decisions which are good for Canada. Therefore, I will take a few moments to address the Government's commitment in the field of agriculture.
As a Member of Parliament from Ontario, I recognize the importance of the promises made in the Throne Speech. While my colleagues will recognize the singularly unique expertise of a Member of Parliament from an urban riding commenting upon agricultural policy, I can assure the House of my sincerity. Ontario is Canada's leading agricultural province with a gross production of over $5 billion, which amounts to over a quarter of the output of Canadian agriculture. Ontario is also the leading food manufacturing province in Canada with 10 per cent of our manufacturing labour force employed in processing agricultural commodities.
My constituents are aware of the problems which have developed in Canadian agriculture over the years, as many of them are employed in the numerous food processing facilities located in the Toronto area. I take particular pride in the Government's accomplishment in respect of the agricultural sector. The Throne Speech has made the strongest commitment to agriculture which has ever been made in a Throne Speech. Many of the problems which exist have been created by subsidies and preferential treatment being given to some commodities in the international market-place. We have pledged to protect Canadian farmers in the face of unfair practices conducted beyond our borders.
October 6, 1986

We were instrumental in having agriculture placed on the agenda of the Tokyo Economic Summit and helped to secure unamimous agreement on addressing subsidies in the new round of multilateral trade negotiations.
The Rural Transition Program has addressed the needs of those farmers who, through circumstance or choice, have decided to seek other occupations by providing counselling, training, and financial assistance during that transition period. We are providing farmers with the real substantial assistance they need to survive difficult times.
The Government's record is there for all to see. The question which begs to be asked is: Are Canadians better off today than they were two years ago? The record shows that the answer is a loud, unequivocal yes. Much still remains to be done, and I am confident that the objectives and directions set out in the Throne Speech, together with the commitment and dedication to accomplish them, will provide a better and brighter tomorrow for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, it is of particular interest to me to participate again in a debate on the Speech from the Throne. As you and all Members in this House are aware, the Speech from the Throne is an opportunity for the Government to lay out to this House and the Canadian people its intentions and its broad vision of the future of this country. It is an opportunity for the Government to explain to the House and the Canadian people what it intends to do in a general sense in the upcoming session. I think all Canadians were somewhat disappointed with this document. I do not think we expected detailed programs to be enunciated in the Speech from the Throne, but I think we did expect a new direction, a new vision to be enunciated in the document.
Certainly the politically wise, meaning the newspaper columnists and people who follow politics actively, speculated that the Speech from the Throne would offer the Government a new opportunity to set forth new directions. It was noted that the Government's popularity in the polls has been declining on a steady basis and that it would use this opportunity to attempt to rally the troops and present a new vision. We did not get much of a vision at all. It was as though a pair of glasses had been put on by the Government and they were full of mist, grease and grime, and some very muddied notions were presented in the speech.
Let us first deal with the question of agriculture. I think commentators in the media have done special pieces outlining the deep crisis which exists in Canadian agriculture today. Various studies have confirmed this. A special committee of this House dealing with agriculture has held extensive hearings as well. We have known for some time that the U.S. Farm Bill would have dramatic effects on the price of grains on the world markets. That is nothing new, Mr. Speaker, the warning has been issued for some time. Thousands of Canadian farm families stand on the brink of bankruptcy. One of the backbones of this nation is in danger. You would have expected that the Party which has enjoyed long support from western Canada and western farmers would have come to the aid of the
farmers in western Canada. You would have expected the Speech from the Throne to have laid out in no uncertain terms that the Government would not allow western Canadian agriculture to slide into bankruptcy.
After all, the Premier of our province, Mr. Grant Devine, a Consersvative, assured the voters in Saskatchewan time and again that he has an agreement with the feds. He was telling us to wait till the Speech from the Throne. In fact, Mr. Devine took an afternoon off from his campaigning to sit in front of the television set to hear of all the goodies the federal Government was going to supply to the western farmers. What a disappointed Mr. Devine we had that day!
According to the Star Phoenix Mr. Devine got on the phone to official cabinet Ministers in Ottawa. He was overheard by a reporter to say over the phone that heads will roll unless the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) delivers on his promises. It was obvious that Mr. Devine was indeed disappointed and that the Speech from the Throne did not deliver on the promises that were made.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, indeed Mr. Devine was desperate. You will remember that earlier this year Mr. Devine said that $5 billion was needed to ensure that western Canadian agriculture would remain viable. If the Government had been really sincere in its commitment it would have thought out this proposal. At least we are talking about big bucks, over $1 billion. The Prime Minister would have had something substantial to announce. He would have had some details. After all, the farmers in my constituency are existing with a tremendous amount of insecurity about their future. They do not need federal politicians to jerk them around. They want some definite answers. Their livelihood is at stake. They do not want to be pawns in some political game that the Tories are playing between Ottawa and Regina. It is serious, Mr. Speaker, it is their livelihood. It is not something to smirk about or to jerk them around with as the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) did when he said, "Well, anything to win an election", grin, grin. And then afterwards he said, "Oh, no, I didn't mean it. I'm sorry, we're really sincere". We do not need the grins that we are seeing on the government benches today. It is serious. There are young farm families on the verge of bankruptcy and unless there is a real commitment by the Government they will go under. There are
October 6, 1986

thousands of these farm families across the Prairies that are on the verge of bankruptcy. These farm families have supported the Tories election after election. These farmers felt that the former Liberal Governments had totally betrayed them and ignored them, and they had. However, lo and behold, this bunch today is exactly the same as the Liberals were before. The farmers have become pawns in the political games the Governments are playing.
The Government did not have any trouble bailing out the banks. Over one weekend a group of bankers came together, stated their problem and got an easy solution. Western farmers need, want, and demand some answers, not more meetings, not more poppycock, not more committees, proposals, suggestions or studies. They want action, Mr. Speaker. It is willing to lose billions of dollars in tax breaks. However, despite his comments in this House on Friday, he would not be precise and it is clear the Government does not have a plan. I wonder whether my colleague can perhaps elucidate the meaning of those comments? Are prairie farmers going to receive money for deficiency payments? Will it be new money? Is this simply a political piece of opportunism on the part of the Government which is concerned about its Conservative colleagues in the Province of Saskatchewan? Is there a genuine desire on the government side to ensure that
October 6, 1986

the desperate plight of prairie farmers is met? Or is their problem in terms of being left almost totally exposed on the world market to competition from the EEC and the United States just going to be ignored by the Government?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly want to thank my colleague for that question. My interpretation of what has been happening is that the Government has no clear idea or program worked through to deliver deficiency payments on the level which is needed by western grain producers.
There was no mention at all in any of the answers that this program will be a deficiency payment program. There was no clear indication that this money will be new money but, rather, it seemed to me to be reshuffled money. There is no indication it is to be zeroed in just on western Canadian farmers. My sense is that the planners, the bureaucrats and some of the larger farmers, the tight groups represented in this Conservative Party, believe that the family farm is a dead entity and should be allowed to die and just fade away, and this is an opportunity for getting rid of some 20,000 or 30,000 farm families in Saskatchewan.
I genuinely believe that some of the thinking behind the Tory inaction emanates from the notion they have that family farming in Canada is not a viable operation and, therefore, we should allow them quietly to die away.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to put a couple of questions to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong). I am mildly confused by some of the rhetoric I heard from him. I confess to not having heard all of it, but I heard enough to pique my curiosity. I believe I heard the Hon. Member going on at great length about what he called the "mismanagement" of the provincial Government in Saskatchewan, how it had ruined the economy, how it had gone into debt, and so on. At the same time it appears that here in Ottawa it is all right for the Hon. Member and his colleagues to call at every opportunity for massive government borrowings in order to assist every area of the economy. Of course, that would have the inevitable effect of raising the deficit and bringing about the kind of irresponsibility the Hon. Member ascribes to the Government of Saskatchewan.
I am curious as to how the Hon. Member can expect to have it both ways. It seems to me he fails to recognize the fact that the Saskatchewan economy is based mainly on agriculture and somewhat on energy. He ignores the fact that both oil prices and grain prices are at historically low levels owing to world prices and to conditions outside of Saskatchewan, conditions over which we have very little control. The Hon. Member knows very well that these historically low prices are not the fault of the Government of Saskatchewan or, indeed, the fault of anyone inside this country. Therefore, I am curious as to how he can gloss over these things and ascribe all sorts of

misery and mismanagement to the Government of Saskatchewan.
